eli5: For a simply supported beam under full uniform load, shear is zero at midspan, so the moment peaks there: M_{max} = w L^{2} / 8. It equals the area under the shear diagram from the support to midspan.
solution:
Reaction = 10(8) / 2 = 40 kN.

M_{max} = \frac{w L^{2}}{8} = \frac{10(8)^{2}}{8} = 80 kN·m, at midspan.

reaction
the force a support pushes back with to hold a structure in place

eli5: For a simply supported beam under full uniform load, shear is zero at midspan, so the moment peaks there: M_{max} = w L^{2} / 8. It equals the area under the shear diagram from the support to midspan.
solution:
Reaction = 12(6) / 2 = 36 kN.

M_{max} = \frac{w L^{2}}{8} = \frac{12(6)^{2}}{8} = 54 kN·m, at midspan.

stem: At a point in a plate, the normal stresses on two perpendicular faces are 80 MPa and 20 MPa (tension positive). The shear stress on those faces is 40 MPa. What is the maximum principal stress?
eli5: Principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on the planes where shear is zero. On Mohr's circle the centre is the average normal stress and the radius is the square root of ((difference/2)^{2} + shear^{2}); the maximum principal stress is centre + radius.
solution:
Centre = \frac{80 + (20)}{2} = 50 MPa.

Radius = \sqrt{(\frac{80 - (20)}{2})^{2} + 40^{2}} = 50 MPa.

Maximum principal stress = 50 + 50 = 100 MPa.

stem: At a point in a plate, the normal stresses on two perpendicular faces are 120 MPa and 60 MPa (tension positive). The shear stress on those faces is 40 MPa. What is the maximum principal stress?
eli5: Principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on the planes where shear is zero. On Mohr's circle the centre is the average normal stress and the radius is the square root of ((difference/2)^{2} + shear^{2}); the maximum principal stress is centre + radius.
solution:
Centre = \frac{120 + (60)}{2} = 90 MPa.

Radius = \sqrt{(\frac{120 - (60)}{2})^{2} + 40^{2}} = 50 MPa.

Maximum principal stress = 90 + 50 = 140 MPa.

stem: A simply supported beam carries a uniform load. Which changes reduce its midspan deflection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a material with a higher modulus of elasticity
Use a deeper section with a larger moment of inertia
Turn a rectangular section on its side so it bends about its weak axis

eli5: A beam sags less if the material is stiffer, the shape is deeper or the span is shorter. Span matters most of all.
solution:
Midspan deflection = \frac{5wL^{4}}{384EI}.

A larger E or a larger I sits in the bottom of the fraction, so each reduces deflection. A shorter L reduces it sharply because L is raised to the fourth power.

More load increases deflection. Bending a rectangle about its weak axis lowers I, which increases deflection.
terms: simply supported
resting on a pin at one end and a roller at the other, so the ends can rotate freely
needs: Mechanics of Materials: Stresses and strains

stem: A cantilever beam carries a point load at its free end. Which changes increase its tip deflection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a material with twice the modulus of elasticity
Use a section with twice the moment of inertia
Use a section with half the moment of inertia

eli5: The tip deflection of a cantilever with an end load is P L^{3} / (3 E I). Anything in the numerator increases deflection and anything in the denominator reduces it, and length counts three times over because it is cubed.
solution:
Doubling the load doubles the deflection. Doubling the length multiplies it by 8. Halving the moment of inertia doubles it.

Doubling E or doubling I halves the deflection.

stem: A steel bar is pulled by an axial force. Which changes reduce its elongation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a material with twice the modulus of elasticity
Replace the steel (E = 200 GPa) with aluminium (E = 70 GPa) of the same size

eli5: A beam sags less if the material is stiffer, the shape is deeper or the span is shorter. Span matters most of all.
solution:
Elongation = \frac{PL}{AE}, where P is the force, L the length, A the cross-sectional area and E the modulus of elasticity.

A and E are on the bottom, so a larger area or a stiffer material reduces the elongation. L is on top, so a shorter bar stretches less.

More force stretches it more. Aluminium has about a third of the stiffness of steel, so the same bar in aluminium stretches about three times as far.
terms: modulus of elasticity
the stiffness of a material: stress divided by strain while the material still springs back

stem: A solid circular shaft 50 mm in diameter carries a torque of 2 kN·m. What is the maximum shear stress?
eli5: Torsional shear stress in a circular shaft grows linearly with radius: stress = T r / J. For a solid shaft J = π d^{4} / 32, so the maximum, at the surface, is 16 T / (π d^{3}).
solution: Maximum shear stress = \frac{16 T}{π d^{3}} = \frac{16(2 × 10^{6})}{π(50)^{3}} = 81.5 MPa.

stem: A metal bar is held rigidly between two walls and heated by 40 °C. Its coefficient of thermal expansion is 12 × 10^{-6} per °C and E = 200 GPa. What compressive stress develops?
eli5: A free bar would lengthen by (coefficient × temperature change × L). The walls prevent that, which is the same as compressing the bar by the same strain. Stress = E × coefficient × temperature change, independent of length and area.
solution:
Restrained strain = 12 × 10^{-6} × 40 = 480 × 10^{-6}.

Stress = E × strain = (200,000 MPa)(480 × 10^{-6}) = 96.0 MPa (compression).

stem: The principal stresses at a point are 120 MPa in tension and 40 MPa in compression. What is the maximum in-plane shear stress?

stem: A thin-walled cylindrical tank has a radius of 500 mm and a wall thickness of 10 mm. The internal pressure is 2 MPa. What is the hoop stress in the wall?
eli5: In a thin-walled cylinder the circumferential (hoop) stress is p r / t and the longitudinal stress is p r / (2 t). The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, which is why such vessels split along their length.
solution: Hoop stress = \frac{p r}{t} = \frac{2(500)}{10} = 100 MPa. The longitudinal stress is half of that, 50 MPa.

stem: A simply supported beam spans 10 m. A uniform load of 6 kN/m covers the first 4 m from the left support only. What is the maximum bending moment?
eli5: The maximum moment is where the shear is zero. Under a uniform load the shear falls by w for every metre, so it reaches zero a distance (left reaction) / w from the left support. The moment there is the area of the shear triangle up to that point.
solution:
Left reaction = \frac{6(4)(10 - 2.00)}{10} = 19.200 kN.

Zero shear at \frac{19.200}{6} = 3.20 m, inside the loaded length.

M_{max} = \frac{1}{2}(19.200)(3.20) = 30.72 kN·m.

eli5: The moment is greatest where the shear crosses zero. Similar triangles locate the crossing, and the moment there is the area of the positive shear triangle.

M_{max} = \frac{1}{2}(45)(4.50) = 101.25 kN·m.

eli5: The bar is statically indeterminate, so use compatibility: the part on one side stretches as much as the other side shortens. For a uniform bar each wall takes a share of the load in proportion to the length of the opposite segment.

stem: A square column 120 mm on a side carries a compressive load of 20 kN applied 300 mm from its centroid, on one axis of symmetry. What is the maximum tensile stress on the cross-section?
eli5: An eccentric load is an axial force plus a moment P e. The axial part compresses the whole section by P / A. The bending part adds M c / I in compression on the loaded side and in tension on the far side.
solution:
Axial: \frac{20,000}{14,400} = 1.389 MPa compression.

Bending: \frac{M c}{I} = \frac{6 P e}{b^{3}} = \frac{6(20,000)(300)}{120^{3}} = 20.833 MPa.

Far face: 20.833 - 1.389 = 19.44 MPa tension.

Axial: \frac{28,000}{18,225} = 1.536 MPa compression.

Bending: \frac{M c}{I} = \frac{6 P e}{b^{3}} = \frac{6(28,000)(350)}{135^{3}} = 23.899 MPa.

Far face: 23.899 - 1.536 = 22.36 MPa tension.

Centre = \frac{80}{2} = 40.0 MPa. Radius = \sqrt{40.0^{2} + 30^{2}} = 50.00 MPa.

Maximum principal stress = 40.0 + 50.00 = 90.0 MPa.
